items.question: How do you understand Jensen Huang's approach to sustaining long-term research projects like NVIDIA's Cosmos world model?
items.object: Jensen Huang's approach to long-term research
items.answer: After we finished Cosmos 1, we asked Jensen whether we should keep going. Jensen told me, 'Just keep going until Cosmos 97,' because he is a very disciplined person. Even if something is important, he will tell you to pace your steps — to keep your rhythm; in other words, not to rush. He is good at fighting marathon battles. Every day, he feels as though the company has only 30 days of cash flow left and will go bankrupt after 30 days.

items.question: Why did you believe deep learning would become the primary way to generate video when you joined NVIDIA?
items.object: Deep learning as the future of video generation
items.answer: When I joined NVIDIA, my goal was this: in the job talk I gave when selling myself to NVIDIA, 10 years ago, I said that one day the primary computation used to generate video would be deep learning. It would not be traditional computer graphics. At that time, computer visual effects and film visual effects used graphics — traditional graphics pipelines to produce beautiful graphics; that was the mainstream. I was among the early people in the field who believed deep learning was the future trend. I remember that in my presentation to our chief scientist, Bill Dally, I talked about deep learning, because it is data-driven and can do many things that traditional graphics cannot. For example, one day I could use a novel as input, put it into deep learning, and it would produce a movie. You could achieve many kinds of control that traditional graphics currently require a great deal of human labor to achieve. At the time, the company was very interested in this, and I was honored to join NVIDIA. After joining, I kept working in that direction.

items.question: How do you see GauGAN's significance in establishing NVIDIA's identity as an AI company?
items.object: GauGAN's significance for NVIDIA
items.answer: When I joined NVIDIA, NVIDIA was not a company generally recognized as an AI company. Deep learning was not yet as hot as it is now. NVIDIA had traditionally worked on computer architecture and designed GPUs; no one was doing more application-side scientific research. I was, in effect, among the early people who built this direction up at NVIDIA. I worked on many things. One piece of work was called GauGAN. It seems to have been translated into Chinese as Ma Liang's Magic Brush: like a little painter, you paint a few colors, each representing a different semantic category, and after painting, it can become a beautiful landscape. That work, in effect, helped NVIDIA establish an image: it could not only make very good GPUs, but also very good AI models. At the time, I also had some colleagues working together on research in the StyleGAN direction. We were the group that, as one of the first groups at NVIDIA — in effect the first — brought this kind of generative network into media generation.

items.question: How did OpenAI’s release of DALL·E change your thinking about your ambition to turn a novel into a movie?
items.object: OpenAI’s DALL·E release and Liu’s ambition to turn a novel into a movie
items.answer: When I gave that job talk 10 years ago, I wanted to tackle the problem of turning a novel into a movie. But at the time, I thought that problem might take a very long time to solve. More precisely, I had not realized that we already had the conditions for it. When your compute and your data are sufficient, you can make such a major breakthrough. But at that time I was busy making digital humans and all sorts of interesting applications. Then one day OpenAI released DALL·E, the earliest text-image model work. Only then did I realize that my ambition was not big enough. I was not brave enough and did not have the determination to make this happen, even in the place with the most compute. At the time, NVIDIA worked this way: to get Jensen to invest compute in you, you had to explain why it was important to the company. I remember that when DALL·E came out, I wrote Jensen a letter telling him that the future was already clear: image generation would be done with deep learning. Many NVIDIA customers used NVIDIA GPUs and traditional graphics to generate images. We could not fall behind in generating images with deep learning. We had to invest GPUs in our team to help this field grow.

items.question: What were you trying to achieve through NVIDIA’s Picasso AI foundry project?
items.object: NVIDIA’s Picasso AI foundry project
items.answer: During that period, I also had a lot of collaboration with Getty Images. Because I had always worked in this direction, these traditional content companies were also very interested in AI, but they were just trying it out and did not have enough determination. After seeing DALL·E, I wrote Jensen a letter asking for GPUs, and wrote Getty Images, a visual-asset provider, a letter saying that we should collaborate, because that was how they could secure their future. Then we reached a collaboration plan: they would provide data, we had compute, and we would build large models for text-to-image. That was the point at which I entered large models. At that time we established a project called Picasso. Our goal was to build an AI foundry. Some companies have data, but they do not have AI talent or AI infrastructure. But they have data and customers. We would help them create a GenAI model, then give them the model so that they could serve their customers, allowing both sides to profit together. At the time, we did this with Getty Images and Shutterstock, a royalty-free image library. This was still work within the Deep Imagination Research team. As we did it, my research gradually became not just about producing a model or producing a paper; we also produced a product that could help customers succeed. This was how it developed step by step.

items.question: How did you come to see NVIDIA's Cosmos world-model project as requiring your full commitment?
items.object: NVIDIA's Cosmos world-model project
items.answer:
When Sora came out, I was very happy, but I again felt that my determination really was not enough. At the time, several of us working in this field wrote a letter to Jensen together, saying that we needed much more investment. That is where the Cosmos project came from. We decided to build a world model, believing it would be an important technology for the company and for humanity. Jensen then asked Sanja Fidler and me to lead this Cosmos effort together.

At that time I had originally been working on Picasso — an AI foundry for media generation — while also being responsible for Cosmos. Later, I felt that the Cosmos project was more important to the company. There was no way around it: I did not have the capacity to split myself between two major projects. Gradually, I wound down the Picasso project and helped those customers find other technology companies that could continue supporting them. Then I focused fully on Cosmos.

After working on Cosmos for a while, we went from 1 to 2 to 3. During this period, more and more customers used it. It needed a certain scale to make the Cosmos project well. You can think of it this way: when I was in Research, it may have been like a germination stage. Once Cosmos was relied on by so many people, whether external customers or internal company teams, it reached a stage where it could not die — it had to succeed. The resources required became much larger. At the beginning of this year, I left NVIDIA Research. I now report to our senior VP of software, one of the biggest leaders in the company. Previously I reported to Bill Dally.

items.question: How do you understand OpenAI's decision to pull back from Sora and concentrate its resources on coding?
items.object: OpenAI's decision to pull back from Sora and concentrate on coding
items.answer: Sora was a major research effort and of course had many applications itself. OpenAI is a very ambitious company. They have a great deal of talent. Sam Altman has always been, since his early days at Y Combinator, an investor. Naturally, he hopes to have that investor mindset: a company should have all kinds of projects, some highly successful, a diverse portfolio. I think over the past year they have faced enormous competitive pressure from Anthropic. They saw Anthropic generate huge economic benefits in coding agents. And when you chat with ChatGPT, the number of tokens you generate may be finished in at most a minute. A coding agent can work for 24 or 48 hours; its token volume is extremely large. They felt this was a very good direction, so they concentrated the company's energy on coding. The Art of War says, 'When forces are spread too broadly, strength is diluted.' Everyone's resources are limited. They readjusted resources toward coding. I do not think they believed Sora was not good work. I simply think that at this point, their company had more important things it had to do, so it had to make a difficult decision.

items.question: Why do you think NVIDIA needs to conduct its own application research to build good AI infrastructure?
items.object: The role of research at NVIDIA
items.answer: Our infrastructure has to be good. The definition of being good is that it suits these application companies' needs. If we do not make these applications ourselves, we cannot understand at all what they need. So we have to travel paths they may take and understand from within. Moreover, designing chips and computer architectures has a very long cycle. We cannot say, 'I will change it immediately now.' It takes a long time to plan. So we need to do this research and invest alongside them, to understand what potentially important problems need solving, so that I can design better chips and better infrastructure to meet the needs of these large AI companies.

items.question: What do you see as the purpose of NVIDIA making open-source models?
items.object: NVIDIA's decision to make open-source models
items.answer: I always feel that if every ambitious, idealistic person in the world had tools to make what they want to make, the world would be better. On one hand, seeing breakthroughs made by OpenAI, Anthropic, and several major Chinese companies makes me very happy. But our society will have an endless stream of ambitious young people, and we hope they have their opportunities too. We can make these models and share them with them. They can make excellent applications, excellent derivative models, or draw inspiration from them to make better models of their own. Different ideas can all be put into practice. I think that when so many diverse ideas have a chance to be realized and presented to users, people have more choices, and social progress can be better. This is why NVIDIA makes open-source models.

items.question: How do you view the possibility that NVIDIA's open-source models compete with your customers?
items.object: NVIDIA's open-source models and competition with its customers
items.answer: When we make these things, especially open-source models like these, we basically put them online at no cost so everyone can use them. In practice, to really deploy them and meet customers' needs, there is still much to do. Especially in embodied AI, many hardware problems and business problems must be solved. I think we are giving the community a signal that we will help them in this area. When you see the trend and our commitment — when we go from generation 1 to generation 2, then 2.5, then 3, generation by generation — you see us moving step by step, trying to make this area better so that everyone can more confidently expect that NVIDIA will keep investing and keep improving here. Once people have that understanding and confidence, they can put their resources into the more important cutting edges and make major contributions. Because every company, even a very rich one, has limited resources. If you do not identify the pain points and key points in which to invest and improve, it is not easy to stand out. Embodied AI is so difficult, with so many things to solve. I think the models we make help them share part of the pressure. I do not see it as competition; I see it as helping everyone succeed.

items.question: Why did you choose to work on embodied world models rather than large language models or world simulators focused on content creation?
items.object: Choosing embodied world models as NVIDIA's research direction
items.answer: Large language models were already developing very well at the time. Also, my background is not in large language models; I come from computer vision — CV. So naturally I had always been around media, around images and video. That was probably my background leading me down this path. Of course, because of my background, the partners who worked with me had similar backgrounds, so we went in this direction. That is why we did not pursue large language models. Also, NVIDIA has a very strong large language model team. I did not feel I could contribute much there. I think Nemotron is getting better and better. On my side, I mainly wanted to solve problems that were more suitable for me to solve. When Sora first came out, it was also a world simulator, but its main applications were more like creative applications. Creation is very interesting. Everyone wants to tell stories in better ways and present what they have in mind — to make it concrete, to help others understand the world they see. That is a good application. But at the time we also saw that Digital AI was developing extremely fast, while society simultaneously had many problems that needed Physical tools — tools that can truly change states in the physical world — to address them. For example, when people get older, they may no longer be able to drive. But when they cannot drive, their quality of life drops substantially. If there are autonomous vehicles, older people can still have mobility. Also, many jobs are very labor-intensive and very dangerous. If robots using this kind of Physical AI could help do them, they could improve people's lives as well. And there are always a pile of trivial matters at home: clearing the dishes, tidying up. These are not necessarily what you most want to do at home. If a robot can help do these things, it improves quality of life. We saw the contribution that world models could make to Physical AI, so we went in the Physical AI direction rather than the content-creation route.

items.question: How do you understand Jensen Huang’s expectations for your Physical AI team at NVIDIA?
items.object: Jensen Huang’s expectations for NVIDIA’s Physical AI team
items.answer: Jensen's requirements for the team are very strict. The goals are high. Of course, the first goal is to help customers. This is not easy, because NVIDIA is a computing company, an AI infrastructure company. What we do best is the entire compute stack, from the underlying infrastructure to CUDA and all the way up. But we are not a solution company — one that provides a robot solution or solutions for other applications. Yet our goal is to help companies building solutions succeed. Sometimes it can feel a little like scratching an itch through a boot. Because you do not really know where the pain points are. When you design a model or a product, if you do not understand your customers, you cannot optimize it. That is why I often come to China: to understand the problems everyone is encountering. How to help them. Of course, that is one difficulty, one of Jensen's requirements. The things we make need to make an impact. Jensen often says he likes this kind of zero-billion-dollar business: it can be unprofitable, but when the business succeeds, it must be very influential and huge. You cannot be satisfied with earning 100 million a year. At that scale, it is huge for many companies, but for NVIDIA, that is not worth a distraction — it is a diversion. You need to solve the most important problems and make the greatest contribution. We believe Physical AI is a problem large enough to make the greatest contribution. So in this direction, you have to be very careful and solve the most important problems, rather than solve things that may produce short-term results but do not have much impact. That is one issue. And of course, you have to make the best. That is also very difficult.

items.question: What made U.S. graduate research seem like the right path for you when you were studying wireless communications?
items.object: Choosing U.S. graduate study over continuing in wireless communications
items.answer: After studying wireless communications there for a while, I came to understand better how it worked. Among my classmates who studied at National Chiao Tung University with me, studying wireless communications, many stayed in Taiwan, China, to do work Taiwan itself was good at — for example, some went to MediaTek or TSMC. At that point I started to wonder whether that was really the path I wanted to choose. Because from childhood through then, I had actually never thought I would go to the United States to study. I had not really valued my English; I felt it was enough to be good at mathematics and physics. During that period, I began to wonder what path was right. In my junior year, I became curious and looked into what U.S. graduate schools and PhD programs were doing. I looked at what I had done at National Chiao Tung University in Taiwan, China, and then I realized the work was very different. I felt I had been calculating how to design a protocol to make transmission faster. I felt that was an improvement, but not a zero-to-one change. Looking at work at those higher-education institutions in the United States, I felt that every success there seemed to be a zero-to-one change. So I felt I should go out and take a chance. I remember telling my parents that I wanted to study in the United States, and they were startled, because they had known me for more than 20 years and had never heard me say I wanted to study in the United States.

items.question: What drew you from quantum communications into computer vision when you began your research career?
items.object: The appeal of computer vision and the decision to switch from quantum communications
items.answer: What I wanted to study in the United States then was quantum communications, because I thought it was magical: relying on quantum mechanics to directly transmit information from A to B. But before going to the United States, I spent a year at Intel in Taiwan, China, where I met a friend. We were both interns there. He worked on image recognition. That was my first exposure to AI, because before then I had only studied communications. I saw him doing image recognition and thought it was magical. He could determine from these pixels what was in them — who it was, what object it was. I began to form an impression of AI and computer vision. I was accepted to the University of Maryland in the United States and began my PhD there. The earliest computer vision did not work very well. Most research funding was from defense. Maryland is very close to Washington, D.C., so at the time some extremely capable early leaders in computer vision and AI were gathered there. When I arrived at that school, I had originally planned to research quantum communications. Later I discovered computer vision work there, on topics close to what I had seen during my Intel internship. I felt that looked more interesting, so I found my advisor, Rama Chellappa. He was, in effect, a pioneer in the field. I began learning AI and computer vision with him. My first topic was to look at a person's gait in video and determine who the person was.

items.question: How do you view the foundation you gained from studying traditional computer vision before deep learning emerged?
items.object: Traditional computer vision as a foundation for AI research
items.answer: Early on, I worked on image recognition and video recognition, and later during my PhD I learned how to use things called shape matching and segmentation, common AI computer-vision research in the understanding direction. I gradually entered AI. There was no deep learning then; it was the era of traditional computer vision. Traditional computer vision — nothing worked at the time, so you had to learn everything. We worked on support vector machines, a very traditional machine-learning approach. Support vector machines are closely related to optimization. You had to learn all kinds of optimization, whether continuous or discrete, as well as graphical models, energy minimization, and all kinds of 3D calibration. I learned quite a lot. I think it was a very solid foundation. But in the year I graduated, ImageNet and AlexNet came out and changed the whole world.

items.question: Why do you see generation as part of understanding?
items.object: Generation as a form of understanding
items.answer: Richard Feynman said, 'If I cannot create, I cannot understand.' When you can generate it, you truly and thoroughly understand it. I think it is somewhat like human learning. When you can explain something, that means you already understand it. Also, early computer vision distinguished between discriminative models and generative models. A discriminative model does not actually have generative capability, but it can determine whether this is A or B. A generative model can likewise be used for discrimination, but it also includes the ability to reconstruct the signal, to describe it. When you can describe it clearly, people may consider that you understand it better.

items.question: How has your view of mathematical beauty in AI research changed?
items.object: Mathematical beauty in AI research
items.answer: Early on, I liked beautiful mathematics. Because in the early stage of computer vision, nothing worked. Computer vision used a great many optimization algorithms. Optimization is about finding the optimal solution. In continuous cases, you often encounter non-convex problems, where you cannot find the optimal solution. In discrete cases, you have NP-hard problems, where you also do not have enough compute to find the optimal solution. But you still research algorithms to find an answer, without knowing how far it is from the optimum. To ensure, with some guarantee, that your answer is not too far from the optimum, you prove what is called a bound. Perhaps the optimal solution is not found, but the answer you find may be only 4% or 20% away from the optimum. That is better than an arbitrary answer. To prove such a bound, early research often began by making assumptions — assumptions that made the mathematics cleaner and made it possible to find an answer, but also moved you further from reality. Early on, I was somewhat inclined to pursue mathematical beauty while overlooking the distance from the real world. After some time, I understood that this was not the right approach, because AI itself is an applied science: intelligence is meant to be applied. I increasingly like getting close to the essence of the problem, rather than being beguiled by fancy mathematics.

items.question: How do you think about making collaboration work in large-scale AI research?
items.object: Collaboration and communication in large-scale AI research
items.answer: Especially after I started making large models, I came to understand that unity and collaboration are extremely important. Communication between people is actually a highly complex problem. For example, I do not know — call it N squared. Suppose you have N people; your communication with these other N people is N squared. N squared is bad complexity-wise; it is not easy to scale. When you have many people, if everyone has to communicate point to point, it is difficult. Better is N, or linear or sublinear. I began to understand that when you need everyone to unite and cooperate to make some huge contribution, you must explain things very clearly so everyone can understand and align on the goal. It is not only that you yourself can make things; you also want everyone to understand what is being made and move in the same direction. This requires much more work to help everyone understand why it matters. This is something I later found extremely important in research, especially research at large scale. You need to make applications, sell your work, and collaborate as a team.

items.question: What did you take away from your experience introducing GauGAN to the public?
items.object: Introducing GauGAN to the public
items.answer:

He asked me what it was called. I said SPADE. He did not like it; it was not easy to understand. It was not user language. Ha.

We had a marketing genius in the company. At that time, all the algorithms were some-GAN. It was the GAN era. That marketing person, Greg Estelle, proposed GauGAN. Gauguin was French. Once the name was proposed, everyone thought it made sense: a painter, a famous painter. The application at the time was also painting, and that was how it came about.

Originally, Jensen was going to announce it at the GTC keynote. But that year he had too many products to introduce. I remember rehearsing with him on Sunday evening, preparing to give a demo on stage. That night, I received a notice saying that there were too many products to discuss and he had decided at the last minute not to include GauGAN in his keynote. We still did a press release and many demos for media friends to see, but it was not in his conference presentation. After many media friends saw it, it instead became the most watched work at GTC.

We made an online app for everyone to try. We got a lot of very good feedback from people using it, and we increasingly moved in the direction of applications.

items.question: How do you understand the role of the information bottleneck in your CoupledGAN work?

items.question: How do you understand the difficulty of controlling image and video generation with text compared with visual signals?

items.answer: There are sketches, meaning drawings. Another signal is segmentation: like a little painter, one color represents a mountain, another represents water. Then there are class labels, for example, saying this is a mountain, this is a car, this is a motorcycle. The most sophisticated and closest to human natural language is text: text-to-image, text-to-video. This is the most natural form. items.question: How did your thinking about scalability lead you to move your team away from GAN research?
items.object: Scalability and the decision to stop researching GANs
items.answer:
During my PhD, I had learned traditional computer vision. After my PhD, the deep-learning era arrived. At the time, I thought you should not do handcrafted algorithm design or handcrafted feature engineering; you should be data-driven. I also understood that a more scalable approach — a simple, scalable approach — is more likely to succeed. So I often told myself that, when making choices, I should find the more scalable option. Later, people called it the bitter lesson.

I was happy working on GANs, but I kept thinking about whether GANs were scalable. Everyone knew GANs were hard to train. I worried that they might ultimately not be scalable. When Jia-Bin Huang came to intern with me, the topic we researched was scaling GANs. It was still very early then. I saw his immense talent. Although we did not write a paper at the time, the volume of experiments was astonishing. Seeing his ideas, I thought, wow, you can think that way too. For example, a GAN then had a generator and a discriminator. I was fortunate to have a very large number of GPUs, enough to train GANs on a cluster. He came up with putting one discriminator on each GPU, but with different weights, so it was like many people simultaneously competing against the generative network. In that era, implementing this was very difficult.

There was another intern then, Jeremy Bernstein. When he interned with me, our research direction was how to use better algorithms to make GANs stable. In the end, neither direction succeeded. It was a very happy period. I learned a great deal. At some point, after working very hard with so many smart people to research how to make GANs more scalable, every result led to the conclusion that GANs were not scalable. I had built this team; everyone joined because they wanted to do GANs. That year I told everyone: we cannot do GANs anymore. This direction is not scalable. At the time we saw diffusion and thought, wow, this method is extremely stable.

items.question: How do you make sense of your earlier research as computer vision moves through successive computational paradigms?

items.answer: I have found that it keeps getting simpler. items.question: Why did you see NVIDIA as the right place to pursue your deep learning research when you left Mitsubishi Electric?
items.object: Choosing NVIDIA as a research workplace
items.answer:
After I began working on deep learning, I believed strongly in compute. Mitsubishi Electric was not a company that valued compute. It was a company that valued algorithms. At the time, in order to do research—to do good research—I often asked my manager to buy GPUs. In meetings I would say, “We need GPUs to do this.” At Mitsubishi Electric, I had a long-term mentor named Oncel Tuzel, also a very well-known researcher. At the time, he decided to leave and join Apple to work on autonomous vehicles. Then I suddenly felt that the main reason I had stayed at Mitsubishi Electric was gone. I began thinking: should I change jobs too?

The natural way to change jobs was to go to Silicon Valley and talk to these big companies. At the time everyone looked at Google, Apple, Amazon, Meta—those big companies. Later, their recruiters found me. I looked and thought, “NVIDIA.” Right—every time I wanted to buy their GPUs. I lacked GPUs so badly and wanted them so much. Why not join a company that actually makes GPUs? So in the end I decided to join NVIDIA. My parents did not really understand at the time, because NVIDIA was a company they had never heard of. They said, “Apple is good. Google is good. Why join this NVIDIA?”

I thought: GPUs are the most important thing, especially then. I had begun working on CoupledGAN, which was an unsupervised approach. An unsupervised approach means data is easier to obtain because you do not need labels. I felt the most important things were compute and data. Since the data did not need labeling, I would go where the compute was.

items.question: What did the changes at Mitsubishi Electric Research teach you about aligning blue-sky research with a company’s interests?
items.object: Aligning blue-sky research with a company’s interests
items.answer:
The Mitsubishi Electric example had a major impact on me. Mitsubishi Electric was very important in the 1990s because it was an early place where unrestricted research could be done. Many famous people in the field were there—Bill Freeman, for example, was at Mitsubishi Electric Research. Bill Freeman attracted a group of famous professors, such as Joe Mark; they had all interned there and did major research. At the time it could compete with Microsoft Research. But at a certain point the company’s direction changed. It began questioning the impact of blue-sky research on the company, and it became increasingly hard to justify paying those researchers. Then something well known happened—something younger people today have not encountered. Important scholars at Mitsubishi Electric began to be fired or leave one after another. Some joined Microsoft; some became professors at universities such as MIT and Harvard; some went to Disney. People gradually left. Some of those who remained continued doing similar research, but it became harder to relate it to the company’s direction. For instance, Mitsubishi Electric was interested in cameras, industrial cameras, and robotic arms. If you helped research those areas, you could obtain company support and continue.

By the time I joined, all of that was already over. But my training taught me that blue-sky research can also align with a company’s interests. Having spent a long time in industry, I often see this cycle: many companies initially give lots of freedom, and many interesting ideas emerge. But after a period, they tighten up and retain a group more related to the company’s interests. You can see this process at Google and Meta alike. I may have been fortunate to see it happen early in my career.

So when I was at NVIDIA, I always believed first, that what I was doing—using deep learning to generate images—was absolutely positively related to the company. I put more thought into understanding how to explain to the company’s decision-makers why it mattered. This is particularly important. Perhaps when a company is in an upswing or expansionary phase, it permits much blue-sky exploration. But once it is in a downward phase, it contracts and will certainly require you to answer: why is what you are doing important? What does it have to do with me? Doing deep learning is very expensive. So you need to focus even more on explaining why it is an important investment for the company.

For instance, Mitsubishi Electric was interested in cameras, industrial cameras, and robotic arms. If you helped research those areas, you could obtain company support and continue.

By the time I joined, all of that was already over. But my training taught me that blue-sky research can also align with a company’s interests. Having spent a long time in industry, I often see this cycle: many companies initially give lots of freedom, and many interesting ideas emerge. But after a period, they tighten up and retain a group more related to the company’s interests. You can see this process at Google and Meta alike. items.question: Why do you think integrating AI with a company’s ecosystem matters as model capabilities converge?
items.object: AI model convergence and integration with a company’s ecosystem
items.answer: When doing AI, everyone pursues better and better models. But gradually you realize that model performance converges; everyone becomes roughly similar. Some people say it keeps improving, but what you see is Anthropic being better this month, GPT better next month, and Gemini perhaps catching up the month after. China’s powerful companies—GLM, Kimi, Seed, Alibaba, Hunyuan, DeepSeek, MiniMax—are all continually making breakthroughs. Gradually, everyone’s models will have roughly similar capabilities. When model capabilities are all similar, you understand that relying purely on the model is not enough. Perhaps I was fortunate to believe early that models would converge. I have always valued not relying only on the model, but integrating it with the rest of the company’s ecosystem. Look at how well Gemini does: Google has a whole suite of Google Docs, Search, and an integrated platform around it. The more people use your model, the more feedback you receive; the more convenient it becomes, the easier it is to contribute to the company. As you contribute more, the company is willing to invest more in you, and you make better models. That lets you sustain long-term development all the way through.

items.question: How has your understanding of what makes research valuable changed?

items.question: How do you assess the idea that a frontier AI company could gain an overwhelming technological lead through exponential growth in intelligence?
items.object: Competition and convergence among frontier AI companies
items.answer: Of course I am curious, and I use these models myself. I see them continually improving. But some people always say there will be exponential growth next, and that if you do not quickly invest in or join these companies, you will miss out on the opportunity. I think history shows this has never happened: one company has never controlled all technology while every other company was unable to catch up. That has never happened in the world, and I do not think AI will be an exception. Everyone is smart. People move around. Someone works at Company A for a while, feels their talent is not recognized, and may move to Company B. This know-how naturally diffuses throughout the field. I do not think one company will achieve an enormous lead over all others. I do not think that is itself a stable social state. If we extrapolate, and model intelligence reaches roughly the same level for everyone, what will they compete on next? Integration—integrating with their ecosystems and products.

items.question: How do you think an AI startup should find its opportunity when competing with OpenAI and Anthropic?

items.answer: I do not think you necessarily have to do this: if you start a company now and do exactly the same thing as OpenAI and Anthropic, it is very dangerous. Your funding will absolutely not be as strong as theirs, and you do not have customers—how will you accumulate them? They have such vast resources that they can make things cheaper, and you will not easily catch up. items.question: How do you see Cosmos helping AI generalize in the physical world?

items.question: How did your experience developing Cosmos lead you toward a single world model in Cosmos 3?
items.object: The evolution of Cosmos toward a single world model in Cosmos 3
items.answer:
When we started Cosmos, I emphasized that we had to iterate quickly. I was deeply influenced by DeepSeek, because DeepSeek is an astonishing company. It iterated three times in a year to produce DeepSeek V3. So I kept emphasizing fast iteration. With fast iteration, you can keep improving and make each generation better than the last. But the problem we were tackling was physical-world models. At the time, especially in 2024, it was not very clear what kind of world model would help people; everyone was still exploring. As I said, uses of world models broadly include prediction and understanding: using a video model to predict the future, or making a reasoning model to explain what happened. So at the beginning, we worked with some partners to understand their needs, had some ideas ourselves, built these models, iterated with the partners, and gradually converged.

After we built prediction, which can predict the future, we thought simulation environments are commonly used, but their generated video has a certain gap from real-world data. Could a model help make it more realistic? We did transfer. To explain what happened, we made Reason. At the time there were three. Later, we understood that if I can describe how pixels change, then those pixel changes are actually very close to changes in my actions. So we made something called Cosmos Policy, for a policy model. Gradually, as I said, we found that this is the same world. No matter from what angle you look at it, you are modeling the same world. The model is learning an internal representation of the world: it is learning a representation during a process of compression. Since it is the same thing, there is also the concept of a foundation model whose core idea is a model that can embrace all rivers and learn patterns from all kinds of data. So if you combine the data used to train reasoning, prediction, transfer, and policy, the model’s upper bound is higher. First, you are describing the same world. Second, a foundation model embraces all rivers and combines things. So we gradually moved toward a single model.

There was also an execution problem. I remember when I was building the first version of Cosmos, because I hoped the models could truly help others through collaboration with these partners, I calculated that I might need models A, B, C, D, E, F, G. I worked it out, and at the time I might have needed 22 models. Then I had a meeting with Jensen. I told Jensen I expected to need 22 models. Jensen felt I had worked very hard. He said, “Very good work, very hard.” But then he said, “You know, when Louis Vuitton—LV—reduced the number of products it displayed, sales went up instead. You do not want too many things confusing consumers and preventing them from making a decision.” That affected me greatly. I understood that I myself had a problem: even I could not distinguish whether to use A or B, so others would be even less clear.

There was also difficulty in execution. When each model comes out, we are not finished just because we publish a paper and move to the next one. We must help users use it. Each released model must be maintained and problems solved. When you have several models, it is very hard. “The more troops you deploy, the thinner your strength becomes.” It affects iteration speed. So while building 1 and quickly building 2 through iterations, we understood that this would not last. We decided to build this only-model world model: Cosmos 3. First, it describes the same event, so it can be combined. Second, a foundation model absorbs all kinds of data and combines them. Development also becomes much simpler. So we moved onto the Cosmos 3 path.

items.question: How do you think about the concern that language and visual signals could interfere with each other when you combine them in a foundation model for physical AI?
items.object: Combining language, video, audio, and action in a foundation model for physical AI
items.answer: These signals each have their purpose. Language can bring in human knowledge and help humans communicate with physical AI. Video provides a great deal of visual information; audio provides a great deal of auditory information, describing how the world works. Video can capture the physical operation of the world more precisely; language is instead very difficult for that, right? But the model we ultimately build is meant to serve people. If it does not understand language, you cannot communicate with it. The model is ultimately meant to help machines take action. If it does not understand action, it cannot change the world. That is how I would put it: our purposes differ. My purpose is for this to become a good foundation model for physical AI. You could say that in the distant past there was no language at all. The development of all human civilization came from observing how the world changes. items.question: Why do you believe combining language, video, audio, and action in Cosmos 3 can make these modalities help one another?
items.object: Mutual benefits of combining language, video, audio, and action in Cosmos 3
items.answer:
Over the past year, even more than a year, we have continuously been researching how to fuse these modalities. From various different studies, we got some clues, and in Cosmos 3 we brought them together. For example, in the Cosmos Policy work, we found that combining video and action helps action. When you directly predict action—when we were building world action models—we found that in addition to predicting what action you should take, you also predict the state, that is, the observation, that will result after taking that action. That helps you train proficiently. So we know that predicting video helps action in world action models. Audio can also help video generation. When you know there is a “click” at the point of impact, you know that the moment of contact is that point. So we know these things are mutually complementary.

People who work on video generally know that going from text to video is a process in which the amount of information increases. The demand space grows, which means there are many possibilities. A function with many possibilities is harder to learn. One thing may have ten possible outcomes, so it has no fixed target and is hard to learn. So when making video or images, people find that when your text description is very detailed, it is easier to generate a good video. So you can see that detailed textual descriptions can also help video.

In Cosmos 3, we wanted to combine all those previous things—Cosmos Reason, Cosmos Predict, Cosmos Transfer, and Cosmos Policy. Combining them itself has benefits: the whole thing is simplified. How to combine these signals so that they complement rather than resist one another can be achieved through experiment design and adjustments to data proportions. At the time, we firmly believed that these signals all describe the same world, that they all contain information about how this world works, and that there should be a way to combine them so that they help one another. More information helps you understand the underlying principles of how things work. So we had that belief and started from that direction.

items.question: Why do you see a two-tower architecture for discrete and continuous information as the right choice for Cosmos at this stage?
items.object: Cosmos's two-tower architecture for discrete and continuous information
items.answer: There are many reasons. At the beginning, Cosmos Reasoning was discrete, starting from a vision-language model; Predict, Transfer, and Policy were continuous. So we knew that discrete works for understanding, and continuous works for generation. Putting them together was a very reasonable choice at this stage. Also, there are many ways to use Cosmos, but a common one is post-training. You may use your video-action pairs to train a generator, or you may only want reasoning and use only understanding data from your own domain for training. Having two components that can be combined in this way, while separating the impact of gradients, helps customers use it. If we connected everything together, then generation and understanding would be together. Suppose I now want to change the distribution for generation. During that change, because everything is connected, your data will also change performance on the understanding side. If you did not have two towers and instead had one, then since the understanding side would change while your data did not contain understanding data, it would be easy for that understanding component to be lost. That would be inconvenient for customers. So splitting it into two is meaningfully helpful for use, although relatively speaking it is still not elegant enough, because you still have to decide the architecture in advance. The data should decide how this is done rather than having you make the distinction manually. But at this stage, I think this is more reasonable and better suited to its use. And from this, people can probably guess that our next goal is to simplify it further. Why have two towers when one tower could be enough? But as we move toward the goal of a one-tower setup, we have to consider whether users can easily make use of it. Our goal is to help everyone win, not to create a model ourselves that can do many things. We believe every robot is somewhat different: the number of cameras and the placement of cameras differ; every autonomous vehicle is different. We think we need restraint. Even if we combine them in pursuit of engineering simplicity and perfection, we also have to consider whether users have a way to use it. That is a topic we must study. But relatively speaking, discrete signals are easier to handle. Once they are fused into continuous variables, the processing difficulty rises.

items.question: How do you approach choosing Physical AI training data for Cosmos 3 that can transfer across different robots?
items.object: Transferable Physical AI training data for Cosmos 3
items.answer: Data is a difficulty. It is especially difficult in Physical AI, because every physical form is different. To collect data, without a physical setup you cannot collect the data. At Nvidia it is even more difficult, because we serve all kinds of Physical AI developers and every robot is different. So what we can do is find what is easiest to share in common. I think Physical AI data mainly comes in two types. One is navigation data, going from A to B. The other is manipulation data: how to use a hand or tool to operate and complete a specified goal. Navigation data is easier to handle: how a car moves, how a robot moves—these can all be collected. Even if robot A and B differ, when they move, they are displacing through space, sometimes perhaps with some rotation added, so it is relatively similar. Manipulation is more complex. We found a trend: people are increasingly pursuing robotic arms that are closer to human hands. The argument is that the human world was built for humans, so most tools are suited to being operated by human hands. AI needs massive amounts of data. The easier the data is to obtain, the more readily you can achieve breakthroughs faster. So most data collectors are people; people have hands. So there are two conditions: human-hand-style data collection, and a world mostly built for human hands. That is why we see everyone moving toward human hands today. So in Cosmos 3, we deliberately added egocentric data, including how people see things through their eyes, from a first-person perspective, and how human hands manipulate objects. Because our goal is not to build a robot ourselves, our goal is to help everyone build very good robots. So we have to find the things that are easiest to transfer across systems. I think egocentric data is very important for everyone.

items.question: How do you approach organizational design for a team as large as the Cosmos team?
items.object: Organizational design for the Cosmos team
items.answer: I see it this way: it is an organizational-design problem. You want everyone’s goals to align, but you also want everyone to be able to make decisions autonomously. When everyone’s goals align but no one can make decisions, progress is very slow, because only a small number of decision-makers can decide. If only I can make decisions—only I can decide how to adjust the data proportions, only I can decide the architecture—then our model will not succeed, because my knowledge and time are limited. What we need is for everyone to be able to make decisions that are important to the organization and to model development. The second thing is that if everyone can make decisions but their goals are not aligned—if I only want to make action good and completely do not care how video performs, or I only want to make understanding good and completely do not care about the rest—then things will diverge. Different architectures may emerge, and it may further lead to horse-race behavior. I think the important thing in running such a large project is to align everyone’s goals while allowing each person to make decisions. In organizational design, I put a lot of thought into creating ways for teams to operate and collaborate, making information transparent so everyone has sufficient information to make the right decisions for the organization. Of course, we also provide room for error, because when people are afraid their decisions will be wrong, they will not make decisions. So you need to let them make decisions, while also accepting that some decisions will be wrong. But when they are wrong, they need to be corrected quickly. All of this takes time and training to let the whole team move in the right direction.

items.question: How has your understanding of what it means to contribute to AI research changed as you have become a manager at Nvidia?

So following that path, I too was initially a highly competitive individual: my work had to be better than yours. That is of course a fine standard—I hope things get better and better. But after a long time, even if you are state of the art for a while, the next thing comes out. Things are constantly improving. My position today is also different. items.question: How do you understand Nvidia’s commitment to helping its customers and ecosystem partners succeed?

items.answer: At the beginning, Nvidia was a design house. In the end, we did not have consumer products; we relied on other companies to help us make GPU cards. items.question: How did Jensen Huang change your thinking about making excuses when solving a problem?
items.object: Jensen Huang’s lesson about making excuses and solving problems
items.answer: I remember once, in a meeting, we were comparing two solutions. I was working on one of them; someone else was working on the other. I remember saying, “I think the setting they used is an unfair setting, so our performance in this respect did not meet our expectations and lagged behind this competing product.” He told me, “Are you a quiet baby?” Nothing in this world is fair. When you are writing papers, you often say, “My setting is different from yours, so they cannot be compared directly.” But if your goal is to solve a problem, then of course you create the conditions needed to solve that problem. If you do not have those conditions, you find a way to get them. But that sentence left a deep impression on me. I hold myself to stricter standards. Making excuses is useless; you have to give everything you have. I had heard this phrase before. Some famous books from West Point also talk about it: no excuse. But when he told me, it made a much deeper impression on me, because after all, he is a well-known figure. I think this phrase had quite a major influence on me. After that, I stopped making excuses.

items.question: How do you see the advantages Chinese robotics companies have in building complete embodied systems compared with companies in the United States?
items.object: Chinese robotics companies' ability to build complete embodied systems

items.question: What do you see as the most important generalization problem that Physical AI needs to solve?
items.object: Generalization of observation-to-action pairs in Physical AI
items.answer: If I could name only one: in Physical AI, the problem of generalization is how to learn the required operation from limited signals and apply it in a scenario it has not seen before. This is the main generalization problem that Physical AI needs to solve: generalization of the observation-to-action pair. This pair's generalization: you see some examples; you see that this action and observation accomplish something. How do you quickly generalize to a new observation and a similar action?

items.question: How do you think Cosmos can help Physical AI builders address the gap between simulation and the real world?

I think better environments have not happened yet. Everyone hopes to create this Matrix, but it has not happened yet. There have been some breakthroughs little by little. items.question: How do you think about the importance of algorithms in AI research now?
items.object: Algorithms, data, and iteration speed in AI research
items.answer: I always thought my algorithms were the best, and the papers I wrote were the most beautiful. You always feel that way. Algorithms are important. You need very good data and very good infrastructure so that you can iterate algorithms quickly. Because even if there are two possibilities: one is that your algorithm is very good at the start—okay, that is good. But even if your algorithm is not good at the start, if you have very good data and very good infrastructure, you can iterate. As long as you follow strict discipline and the principles of controlled experiments, your algorithm will get better and better. So I actually think iteration speed is the most important thing. And iteration speed needs strong infrastructure to support it. Data is very important, because if a problem can be solved with data, just solve it with data. There is no need to develop an algorithm, because data is much simpler. So I do not like wasting effort. If a problem can be solved with data, collect data; create data. Only solve with algorithms what truly cannot be solved that way.
